zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: supplied [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription corrections and English notes are this reviewer's work, not a reproduction of the lexical dataset.

lines.note: Keidaku means a promise or assent, marked as written usage. The damaged capital is Q, matching the preceding page's catchword, not OCR D. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keiha is explained by katamuki yaburu and glossed as falling into destruction. The initial Q is damaged but retains its tail; OCR Beifa is rejected. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keihaku is explained as flattering behaviour, with tsuishō-gamashii koto supplying the Japanese paraphrase. The Portuguese lisonjas begins across this line break.

runs.text: jas, ou actos, & palauras leues com que hum

lines.note: Completes lisonjas and includes superficial acts and words. The relative clause below explains their purpose as pleasing others.
The aim is to please other people. Keihaku wo yū begins the example of saying flattering things; the alternative suru follows on the next row.
The alternative verb suru extends the expression to doing such things. The Portuguese repeats the contrast between saying and doing, with semelhantes divided below.
Completes semelhantes, referring to the flattering words and acts already described. This one-word continuation remains a separate body line.
Keihakuna hito denotes a flatterer or ingratiating person in this entry. The Portuguese Liſõ- carries an abbreviation tilde and continues as lisongeiro below.

runs.text: geiro, ou homem que procura contentar com o-

lines.note: Completes lisongeiro and describes a person who seeks to please. The final o- begins obras, rather than standing as a separate article.
Completes obras and characterizes the person's words as light and affected. Afeitadas is retained in the historical gloss, not replaced with modern wording.
Keihakuni is the adverb corresponding to the preceding flattering adjective. Adu. is the only printed gloss; no unprinted translation is inserted.
Keihai is explained literally as tilting a sake cup. The Portuguese beber begins at the line end and gives the idiomatic drinking sense.

Completes beber copo de vinho, drinking a cup of wine. The final S marks written usage; it is not part of the noun phrase. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

runs.text: O arruinarſe, ou começar a cair, &

lines.note: This separate keihai means falling into ruin or beginning to collapse. It is distinct from the preceding cup-tilting homograph.
The literal sense concerns a building deteriorating or falling down. Keifai- begins the Japanese example and retains its printed terminal hyphen before ni.
Keihai ni oyobu or keihai suru means reaching a state of ruin. A new figurative application begins with the abbreviated Portuguese Item and per met. across rows.

runs.text: met. Deſtruirſe, ou deſfazerſe o gouerno

lines.note: Completes per met. and applies collapse figuratively to the dissolution of government. The governmental unit is specified below.
The gloss concerns a commonwealth's government. Kuni no matsurigoto begins the corresponding Japanese example, with matsurigoto divided after ma-.

Completes kuni no matsurigoto keihai suru, the government of the country falling into ruin. The final S marks the written expression. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keihen means beside a valley, explained by tani no hotori. The roman initial Q replaces the OCR's italic O; Iũto retains its abbreviation tilde. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keihyaku is explained by uyamatte mōsu, speaking respectfully. The headword's initial is Q rather than OCR G, consistent with its repeated example below.

Completes speaking with reverence and gives keihyaku suru. The example reinforces the respectful-speech sense and is marked for written use. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keihō is a law that punishes, or penal law. The headword's caron is kept distinct from the neighbouring long-u form. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keifū means a gentle wind, explained by karui kaze. The initial Q is roman, not an italic O; the final u visibly has a caron. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keiga is joy or congratulation, explained with yorokobi and yorokobu. The dictionary gives the brief noun gloss Alegria and a written-register label. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keigo means a guard or watch. Keigo wo begins the example about stationing guards, with its verb continuing below.
Suyuru completes the expression for setting guards. The next example begins Qei- and continues as keigo no tsuwamono, soldiers on watch.
Completes keigo no tsuwamono and directly glosses it as soldiers serving as watchmen. The historical tçuuamono spelling is preserved.
Keigo suru means guarding or keeping watch. The following row states what the watch is intended to prevent.

runs.text: que ſe não faça algum inſulto, &c.

lines.note: Completes the purpose clause: preventing an assault or outrage. Inſulto retains its historical meaning within the guard-duty definition.
Keigobune are guard or escort boats. The Portuguese describes vessels that go out to provide protection; q̃ retains its abbreviation mark.

runs.text: pera dar guarda, ou defender dos inimigos.

lines.note: The boats provide guard or defence against enemies. The scan has a continuous defender; the OCR's internal separation de fender is removed.
Keigei denotes a whale. The example begins 'in the jaws of the whale' and is completed by kakaru on the following row.

runs.text: Cair na boca da balea, ou ſer comi-

lines.note: The phrase means falling into a whale's mouth or being eaten by it. Comi- is continued as comido, preserving the physical division.
After completing the literal gloss, a figurative example places one's body at the whale's jaws. Agui- continues as agito with the locative particle below.
Completes the figurative phrase about crossing the sea while exposing one's body to peril. The Portuguese explicitly marks the usage as metaphorical.
The crossing involves great risk and danger to life. The printed joined granderiſco is retained rather than normalized to grande risco.

runs.text: Eſcreuer, ou mandar carta falando cõ

lines.note: Keijō means respectfully writing or sending a letter. The abbreviation cõ continues the phrase 'speaking with respect' on the next row.
The epistolary example respectfully announces a brief written message. The printed Ippit retains its final checked t rather than being expanded to ippitsu.

runs.text: Eſcreuo vos hũa breue carta. S.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the example as writing a brief letter to the addressee. Hũa retains its tilde, and S identifies the written formula. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keimei refers to cockcrow. The repeated term begins the time expression keimei no jisetsu, whose remainder occupies the next row.

runs.text: Tempo de madrugada, em q̃ canta

lines.note: Keimei no jixet means the early-morning time of cockcrow. The final t in jixet is preserved; the Portuguese subject gallo follows below.
Completes the first time expression and introduces keimei no jibun with the same dawn sense. The Portuguese translation continues on the following row.

The gloss specifies early morning or dawn. The printed polamanhãa is retained with its joined form and doubled final vowel rather than modernized. Enlargement places the tilde over the first of the two final a letters; this local evidence is retained despite the guide's usual nhaã pattern.

runs.text: Modo de cantar a galinha do ma-

lines.note: Keikeito represents the call of a wild gallinaceous bird. Ma- begins mato, and the following row provides the dictionary's comparative bird-name.
Completes galinha do mato and compares the bird to a Japanese partridge. The historical description is retained without assigning a modern biological species.
Keikei hororo represents the bird's calling and wing-beating together. The Portuguese object asas is carried onto the next physical row.
Completes the bird's wing-beating description. The scan separates the article a from the worn initial g of galinha; OCR agalinha incorrectly joined them.
Keiken pairs a cock and a dog; the Portuguese lists the same animals in reverse order. The headword's worn initial is Q, not OCR D.
Keiki denotes a view or prospect. Keiki no yoi tokoro describes a place with a pleasant view, translated on the next row.
Completes the example as a place with a good view. This is the translation of the Japanese phrase, not a separate headword.
Keikyō means a bridge across a valley, explained by tani no hashi. The Portuguese passar is divided at the physical line end.

runs.text: ſa algum valle da banda dalem. S.

lines.note: Completes the description of crossing a valley to the other side. The entry ends with the written-register label S. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keikyoku refers to thorny growth, with ibara and karatachi as Japanese equivalents. The Portuguese comparison continues with tojos below.
Tojos supplies the second Portuguese term for thorny scrub. It is a real short continuation of the preceding plant entry.
A distinct keikyoku denotes a sleeping chamber, explained by neya and tsubone. Dor- begins dormir in the Portuguese gloss.

Completes casa de dormir, a sleeping room. The short continuation and its written-register label belong to the preceding keikyoku entry. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keikyū means a light leather or fur garment, explained by karuki kawagoromo. The caron on the final u is visible and retained.

Completes the material description as a garment of skins or pelts. The final S marks the expression as written usage. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
This keikwa denotes the flower of a tree. The brief Portuguese definition does not establish a particular botanical species, so none is supplied.
Another keikwa means firefly light, explained by hotarubi. The Portuguese describes light produced by a small creature, continued below.

runs.text: bichinho que luze de noite. S.

lines.note: The creature shines at night, completing the firefly-light definition. The written-register label is retained with the short gloss. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
A third keikwa means the passage of time, explained by hesugosu. Sunẽ begins the example of many years passing; its abbreviation tilde is preserved.

Completes the example sunen keikwa su and glosses it as many years passing. The ß ligature in this Portuguese occurrence remains distinct from Paſſar above. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keikwai is explained by hemeguru, travelling around through different lands. The Portuguese location phrase continues on the next row.
Completes the general definition and gives shokoku wo keikwai su, travelling through the various countries or provinces. The printed historical spelling is retained.

runs.text: Correr por todos os reinos. S.

lines.note: The translation describes travelling through all the kingdoms. The opening C is visibly a capital, correcting the OCR's lowercase form. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keikwan is a crown of thorns, explained by Iguino camuri. The Portuguese espinhos is divided after eſpi-, which remains on this row.

Completes espinhos and closes the crown-of-thorns entry with its written-register label. No separate body entry begins here. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keikwō means firefly light, explained by hotaru no hikari. The caron is preserved; lu- begins the Portuguese insect-name lucerna bicho.
Completes lucerna bicho, the luminous insect in the preceding definition. The printed two-word expression is not merged or replaced with a modern name.
Keira denotes light, fine fabric, explained by karuki usumono. Del- begins delgadas, specifying the thinness of the material below.

Completes delgadas, describing the fabric as fine and thin. The final S closes the written-register clothing term. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keiraku is equated with miyako, the principal city or capital. Miyaco is a Japanese synonym after i, not a term embedded in Portuguese prose.

Completes the definition as the kingdom's metropolis. This refers back to the capital-city headword and bears a written-register label. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keiran means hens' eggs, explained by niwatori no kaigo. The historical caigo is retained rather than replaced with modern tamago.

runs.text: nha. ¶ Item, Hũa certa iguaria que ſe faz

lines.note: After completing galinha, the entry adds a prepared food bearing the same name. The following rows describe its ingredients and egg-like shape.

runs.text: de farinha de arroz, à maneira, & ſemelhã-

lines.note: The preparation uses rice flour and is made in the likeness of eggs. The nasal abbreviation in ſemelhã- is preserved across the physical division.

runs.text: ça de ouos com aſucar, ou jagra dentro.

lines.note: Completes semelhança and specifies sugar or jagra inside the egg-shaped preparation. The source's ingredient names and historical aſucar spelling remain unchanged.
The verb means kicking something into a place, such as water, as the next row confirms. The visible internal gap in Qe ire is retained despite the lexical unity of the verb.
The action is performed with the foot, confirming the kicking sense of Qe ire. The printed grave accent on pè is preserved.
Keiren is compassion or mercy, explained by megumi awaremu. The Portuguese misericordia is split at the physical line ending.
Completes misericordia and supplies piedade as a second gloss. This continuation defines compassion, not the modern homograph for convulsion.
Keireki refers here to the passage of time. The repeated headword begins the example, whose suru is printed on the following row.

Suru completes keireki suru, time passing. The final S labels written usage and the entire short row remains body text. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keiryaku, alternatively keisaku, denotes devising a plan or using ingenuity. The Latin l introduces the alternative and is not a Japanese syllable.
Keiryaku wo megurasu means working out or devising a strategy. The Portuguese translation begins with inventing and continues with planning methods below.

runs.text: traçar modos, & industrias pera algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes the example as devising methods and means for some purpose. The source's industrias concerns ingenuity or contrivance in this context.
Keiriku means killing or putting someone to death by judicial authority. The example's suru is carried to the following physical row.
Suru completes keiriku suru. The row is a Japanese example continuation, not footer furniture despite its short length.
Keisaku is associated with hakari and hakaru, planning or reckoning. The cross-reference is visibly Qeiriacu, correcting OCR Qciriacu and matching the preceding entry.

Keiso pairs a weasel and a rat, directly explained by itachi and nezumi. The Japanese synonyms are not part of the Portuguese prose. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Keisū denotes a young bird, explained by niwatori no hina. The worn final glyph is u with a caron, not OCR t; its precise damaged impression merits retention of this note.

Completes the description as the offspring of a wild gallinaceous bird. The source's comparison is preserved without forcing a modern species identification. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.

Keisui is valley water, explained by tani no mizu. The material below is a signature and catchword, not another body line. The separate S. usage label is printed upright. Typeface update: S. is provisionally italicized under the bulk convention.
Anticipates Qeitat. at the opening of f380. The signature B b b 2 is separately retained as sig-l001; neither item belongs to the body text.
